cards.front: In these autism mouse models, tactile over-reactivity can look the same yet come from different defects. By what three things should each claim about it be located?
cards.back: By the cells manipulated, the mechanism measured and the developmental window tested.
cards.why: Alike-looking phenotypes arise from unlike defects along the early touch pathway, so the manipulation is what fixes the claim.
cards.quote: locate each claim by the cells manipulated, the mechanism measured and the developmental window tested

cards.front: State three things the mouse-model touch results in this lesson do not do.
cards.back: They do not identify one mechanism for autism, do not turn a mouse movement into a reported percept, and do not establish a human developmental window.
cards.quote: It does not identify one mechanism for autism, turn a mouse movement into a reported percept or establish a human developmental window.

cards.front: Criterion B4 of the DSM-5 covers hyperreactivity, {{c1::hyporeactivity}} and unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment.
cards.quote: Criterion B4 of the DSM-5 covers hyperreactivity, hyporeactivity and unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment.
cards.section: First separate the readouts

cards.front: How does the DSM-5 sensory criterion (B4) sit within the restricted and repetitive behaviour criteria for autism?
cards.back: It is one of four such criteria, of which at least two must be met, so no sensory feature is individually required.
cards.quote: It is one of four restricted and repetitive behaviour criteria, of which at least two must be met.
cards.section: First separate the readouts

cards.front: Why does the wording of the DSM-5 sensory criterion mean that not every autistic person is over-reactive to touch?
cards.back: The criterion covers hyporeactivity as well as hyperreactivity, so sensory difference runs in both directions, and no one sensory feature is required for a diagnosis.
cards.quote: Sensory difference therefore runs in both directions, and no one sensory feature is required for a diagnosis.
cards.section: First separate the readouts

cards.front: A human detection threshold, mouse air-puff reactivity and a daily-life sensory report are treated as three different quantities. Why?
cards.back: Each holds something different fixed and measures something different: a reported smallest stimulus, the size of a startle-like movement, and a person's response in context.
cards.why: Because the quantities differ, none of the three can report either of the others by itself.
cards.quote: Three measurements that sound similar ask different questions
cards.section: First separate the readouts

cards.front: In the static finger-vibration task of Puts and colleagues (2014), the autistic cohort's mean detection threshold was {{c1::9.13 micrometres}}, against 6.59 micrometres.
cards.back: Thirty-two autistic and 67 typically developing children aged 8 to 12.
cards.quote: the autistic cohort's mean detection threshold was 9.13 micrometres, against 6.59 micrometres
cards.section: First separate the readouts

cards.front: A cohort's mean vibrotactile detection threshold is higher than the comparison group's. Does that indicate better or poorer detection in the task, and why?
cards.back: Poorer detection. The stimulus had to become larger before it was reported.
cards.why: A higher threshold is a larger stimulus requirement; it neither contradicts nor measures everyday over-reactivity.
cards.quote: Poorer detection. The stimulus had to become larger before it was reported.
cards.section: First separate the readouts

cards.front: Static vibrotactile thresholds were 6.59 micrometres in the typically developing cohort and 9.13 micrometres in the autistic cohort. Give the absolute difference and the increase relative to 6.59.
cards.back: Difference = 9.13 - 6.59 = 2.54 micrometres. Relative increase = 2.54 / 6.59 x 100 = 38.5 per cent (ratio 9.13 / 6.59 = 1.385).
cards.quote: That is a 2.54-micrometre difference, or 38.5 per cent relative to 6.59.
cards.section: First separate the readouts

cards.front: A child is autistic. Can the Puts group means be used to state that child's vibrotactile threshold, or how a touch feels to them?
cards.back: No. The group distributions overlap heavily, so the means set no individual threshold and say nothing about how a touch feels.
cards.quote: The group distributions overlap heavily, so the means do not set any one child's threshold or say how a touch feels.
cards.section: First separate the readouts

cards.front: Orefice and colleagues (2016) tested four mouse lines carrying autism-associated mutations, Mecp2-null, Mecp2R306C, Shank3B heterozygous and Fmr1-null. What did the fixed air puff show at 6 to 8 weeks?
cards.back: All four reacted more strongly than controls to the fixed air puff.
cards.quote: At 6 to 8 weeks, all four reacted more strongly than controls to the fixed air puff.
cards.section: Locate a contribution with conditional genetics

cards.front: In a primary somatosensory neuron, its cell body lies in a {{c1::dorsal-root or trigeminal ganglion}}, and its central terminal lies inside the spinal cord or brainstem.
cards.quote: its cell body lies in a dorsal-root or trigeminal ganglion, and its central terminal lies inside the spinal cord or brainstem
cards.section: Locate a contribution with conditional genetics

cards.front: Which cells does Advillin-Cre supply with Cre recombinase in the mouse, and which does it not?
cards.back: The whole population of dorsal-root and trigeminal neurons that have expressed Advillin at any time, plus sympathetic ganglion neurons. It is not restricted to one mechanoreceptor subtype.
cards.quote: Advillin-Cre supplies Cre recombinase to the whole population of dorsal-root and trigeminal neurons that have expressed Advillin at any time, plus sympathetic ganglion neurons, not to one mechanoreceptor subtype.
cards.section: Locate a contribution with conditional genetics

cards.front: Why can crossing Advillin-Cre to a floxed allele test whether a contribution to a behaviour lies outside the brain?
cards.back: The gene is removed from the targeted sensory neuron, including its central terminal, while resident brain and spinal-cord cells keep their copies.
cards.quote: Crossing it to a floxed allele removes the gene from the targeted neuron, including its central terminal, while resident brain and spinal-cord cells retain their copies.
cards.section: Locate a contribution with conditional genetics

cards.front: In these conditional-deletion experiments, what does it mean to say that gene loss in the targeted population is sufficient for an outcome?
cards.back: That the restricted manipulation can produce the outcome. It does not mean the targeted population is the only route to it.
cards.quote: Here sufficient means that the restricted manipulation can produce the outcome.
cards.section: Locate a contribution with conditional genetics

cards.front: Mecp2 is restored mainly in the Advillin-targeted sensory neurons on an otherwise Mecp2-null background. Which measures moved toward control, and which did not?
cards.back: Tactile sensitivity and selected anxiety-like and social measures moved toward control; lethality, memory and motor deficits did not.
cards.why: The restoration shows that this population can rescue part, not all, of the phenotype.
cards.quote: This population can rescue part, not all, of the phenotype
cards.section: Locate a contribution with conditional genetics

cards.front: An inducible Advillin-CreERT2 line begins sensory-neuron deletion at P28 rather than during development. If the tactile and anxiety-like outcomes had the same developmental requirement, what should happen, and what did happen?
cards.back: They should change together. Instead the tactile deficits still appeared while the anxiety-like phenotype did not, so the two outcomes have different timing requirements in this experiment.
cards.quote: Instead, the tactile deficits still appeared while the anxiety-like phenotype did not.
cards.section: Locate a contribution with conditional genetics

cards.front: A {{c1::low-threshold mechanoreceptor}}, or LTMR, is an afferent that responds to innocuous mechanical stimulation.
cards.quote: A low-threshold mechanoreceptor, or LTMR, is an afferent that responds to innocuous mechanical stimulation.
cards.section: Build the terminal mechanism as an evidence ladder

cards.front: Where in the mouse dorsal horn do GABRB3-containing GABA-A receptors localise?
cards.back: To presynaptic compartments of A-beta- and A-delta-LTMR terminals.
cards.quote: GABRB3-containing GABA-A receptors localise to presynaptic compartments of A-beta- and A-delta-LTMR terminals in mouse dorsal horn.
cards.section: Build the terminal mechanism as an evidence ladder

cards.front: In sensory-neuron Mecp2 mutants, GABRB3 puncta associated with vGlut1-positive terminals fell by about {{c1::70 per cent}}.
cards.back: A punctum is an immunolabelled cluster in fixed tissue.
cards.quote: GABRB3 puncta associated with vGlut1-positive terminals fell by about 70 per cent
cards.section: Build the terminal mechanism as an evidence ladder

cards.front: Immunolabelling shows about 70 per cent fewer receptor-associated puncta at these terminals. Does that establish about 70 per cent lower GABA-A conductance, and why?
cards.back: No. Puncta are counted marker clusters in fixed tissue; conductance is an electrical measurement, and the imaging gives no conversion between them.
cards.quote: Puncta are counted marker clusters in fixed tissue; conductance is an electrical measurement.
cards.section: Build the terminal mechanism as an evidence ladder

cards.front: After sensory-neuron deletion of Mecp2 or Gabrb3, dorsal-root stimulation evoked more asynchronous quantal EPSCs in dorsal column neurons in P14-to-P19 slices. Which side of the synapse does the pattern of change point to?
cards.back: The presynaptic side: frequency rose without a corresponding amplitude change, which supports a change in release rather than in postsynaptic receptors.
cards.quote: Frequency rose without a corresponding amplitude change, supporting a presynaptic change.
cards.section: Build the terminal mechanism as an evidence ladder

cards.front: Why does GABA-A receptor activation depolarise primary sensory afferents rather than hyperpolarise them?
cards.back: These afferents hold chloride high, so the chloride gradient sets the sign of the response and the receptor's opening depolarises the terminal.
cards.quote: Because these afferents hold chloride high, GABA-A receptor activation depolarises them
cards.section: Build the terminal mechanism as an evidence ladder

cards.front: A dorsal root potential is a readout of primary afferent depolarisation. What happened to evoked dorsal root potentials in isolated cords after sensory-neuron deletion of Mecp2 or Gabrb3, and what does that add?
cards.back: They were greatly diminished, which adds a physiological measure of reduced GABA-A-dependent primary afferent depolarisation to the anatomical puncta loss.
cards.quote: Evoked dorsal root potentials were greatly diminished in isolated cords after sensory-neuron deletion of Mecp2 or Gabrb3.
cards.section: Build the terminal mechanism as an evidence ladder

cards.front: Three observations are put together: less receptor-associated marker, more afferent-evoked quantal release and less GABA-A-dependent primary afferent depolarisation. What did the authors conclude?
cards.back: They attributed the touch phenotype to deficient GABA-A-mediated presynaptic inhibition.
cards.quote: The authors attributed the touch phenotype to deficient GABA-A-mediated presynaptic inhibition.
cards.section: Build the terminal mechanism as an evidence ladder

cards.front: Why should the presynaptic-inhibition account stay attached to these LTMR experiments rather than be treated as settled physiology for every sensory afferent?
cards.back: In proprioceptive afferents, later work places axonal GABA-A receptors mainly near nodes and branch points, where they aid spike propagation, and assigns inhibition of release to GABA-B receptors.
cards.quote: Later work in proprioceptive afferents instead places axonal GABA-A receptors mainly near nodes and branch points, where they aid spike propagation
cards.section: Build the terminal mechanism as an evidence ladder

cards.front: What did cultured large-diameter dorsal-root-ganglion neurons from 6- to 8-week-old Shank3 mutants show?
cards.back: Reduced Ih, the hyperpolarisation-activated current, and greater excitability.
cards.quote: Shank3 mutants had reduced Ih, the hyperpolarisation-activated current, and greater excitability
cards.section: Build the terminal mechanism as an evidence ladder

cards.front: Shank3-mutant sensory neurons are more excitable, yet no altered GABRB3 expression was detected at their LTMR central terminals, while Mecp2 and Gabrb3 mutants show the presynaptic GABA-A defect. What follows for the mechanism of tactile over-reactivity in these models?
cards.back: At least two peripheral cellular routes reach the same endpoint, so the phenotype does not identify one mechanism.
cards.why: This rests on the lesson's rule that locus, mechanism and developmental window are separate claims tested by separate manipulations.
cards.quote: No altered GABRB3 expression was detected at Shank3 LTMR central terminals.
cards.section: Build the terminal mechanism as an evidence ladder

cards.front: After a high dose, isoguvacine was detected in blood and liver but not in brain or cerebrospinal fluid. What does that support, and what does it not?
cards.back: It supports poor measured central exposure under those conditions. It is non-detection at stated limits, not proof that no molecule can ever cross.
cards.quote: That is non-detection at stated limits, not proof that no molecule can ever cross.
cards.section: What the route map did not show: the causal control

cards.front: What did low acute doses of the GABA-A agonist isoguvacine do to tactile over-reactivity in mice, and how did that compare with midazolam?
cards.back: They reduced tactile over-reactivity in five genetic models and one maternal-immune-activation model, without the sedation reported for the brain-penetrating comparator midazolam in those assays.
cards.quote: Low acute doses reduced tactile over-reactivity in five genetic models and one maternal-immune-activation model
cards.section: What the route map did not show: the causal control

cards.front: Subcutaneous isoguvacine reduces stimulus-evoked A-beta-LTMR firing recorded from the L4 ganglion in anaesthetised mice. Predict the drug effect after homozygous Gabrb3 deletion in sensory neurons, and say what was found.
cards.back: It should disappear if the drug acts through GABA-A receptors in those neurons. It did: isoguvacine no longer changed touch-evoked spiking.
cards.quote: It should disappear if the drug acts through GABA-A receptors in those neurons.
cards.section: What the route map did not show: the causal control

cards.front: A drug given outside the brain lowers touch-evoked firing in sensory neurons. Design the single genetic control that would place the drug's target in those neurons themselves, and say what the mouse experiment found.
cards.back: Delete the drug's receptor subunit only in sensory neurons and repeat the recording; the effect should vanish. It did, which localised the target to those neurons.
cards.why: This applies the lesson's rule that a restricted manipulation, not the behaviour alone, fixes the locus of a claim.
cards.quote: A receptor deletion in the neuron removed the drug's effect on that neuron.
cards.section: What the route map did not show: the causal control

cards.front: In the chronic isoguvacine experiment, litters received 2 mg/kg daily from P1 to P42. What makes the litter, not the pup, the treatment unit here?
cards.back: Each litter contained mutant and control pups and the whole litter received the same treatment, so treatment was assigned per litter.
cards.quote: Each litter contained mutant and control pups, and the whole litter received the same treatment.
cards.section: What the route map did not show: the causal control

cards.front: Chronic isoguvacine from P1 to P42 improved body condition, some brain abnormalities, anxiety-like behaviours and some social impairments. Which deficits persisted?
cards.back: Texture discrimination and memory deficits persisted, as did Mecp2 motor impairment and Shank3 overgrooming. The effects were selective, not a general rescue.
cards.quote: Texture discrimination and memory deficits persisted, as did Mecp2 motor impairment and Shank3 overgrooming.
cards.section: What the route map did not show: the causal control

cards.front: Tasnim and colleagues (2024) asked which mouse models already over-react to an air puff at P4, measured as maximal body displacement within 500 ms. What did the comparison across models show?
cards.back: Gabrb3 and Mecp2 loss-of-function pups were already more reactive at P4; Nlgn2 and Rorb mutants were not, although both showed tactile abnormalities as adults.
cards.quote: Nlgn2 and Rorb mutants were not, although both showed tactile abnormalities as adults.
cards.section: Timing requires two different designs

cards.front: Where does the Nlgn2 tactile phenotype sit in the touch pathway, and which manipulation placed it there?
cards.back: In a later spinal system: deleting Nlgn2 from dorsal-horn neurons with Lbx1-Cre was sufficient for adult tactile alterations.
cards.quote: Deleting it from dorsal-horn neurons with Lbx1-Cre was sufficient for adult tactile alterations.
cards.section: Timing requires two different designs

cards.front: If Nlgn2 loss weakens dorsal-horn synaptic inhibition, predict what miniature inhibitory currents should show at P19 to P21, and say what was measured.
cards.back: Their frequency and amplitude should fall. In P19-to-P21 Cdx2-Cre Nlgn2 mutants, deleted in all cells below cervical level 2, both measures were reduced in the dorsal horn.
cards.quote: both measures were reduced in the dorsal horn
cards.section: Timing requires two different designs

cards.front: Across the models tested, neonatal over-reactivity went with adult anxiety-like and social differences while later-emerging over-reactivity did not. Why does that not show that the early tactile state causes the later behaviours?
cards.back: It is an association across genotypes, not an intervention on the early tactile state, so genotype differences could carry both ends.
cards.why: Causation would need the early tactile state changed within a genotype, which is why the design problem uses timed deletion and restoration.
cards.quote: That is an association across genotypes, not proof that the early tactile state causes the later behaviours.
cards.section: Timing requires two different designs

cards.front: Air-puff reactivity was sampled at P4 and in adulthood. What can that two-age design establish about onset, and what can it not?
cards.back: It separates early-onset from later-onset models, but it does not identify the onset day.
cards.quote: Sampling two ages does not identify the onset day, although it does separate early-onset from later-onset models.
cards.section: Timing requires two different designs

cards.front: In skin biopsies from 32 autistic men, intraepidermal nerve-fibre density was 5.53 fibres per millimetre against 11.13 in controls. Give the absolute difference and the percentage reduction.
cards.back: Difference = 11.13 - 5.53 = 5.60 fibres per millimetre. Reduction = 5.60 / 11.13 x 100 = 50.3 per cent, so the autistic group's density was about half (5.53 / 11.13 = 0.497).
cards.quote: intraepidermal nerve-fibre density was lower than in controls, 5.53 against 11.13 fibres per millimetre
cards.section: What this does and does not mean for people

cards.front: Why does the lower intraepidermal nerve-fibre density in autistic men not bridge the mouse mechanism described in this lesson?
cards.back: Intraepidermal fibres are small fibres, not the A-beta- and A-delta-LTMRs central to the mouse work, so the measurement is of a different afferent population.
cards.quote: Those are small fibres, not the A-beta- and A-delta-LTMRs central to the mouse work.
cards.section: What this does and does not mean for people

cards.front: What is the clinical status of peripheral GABA-A treatment for tactile over-reactivity in autism?
cards.back: None has been approved. Isoguvacine remains experimental: a 2025 review reported no documented human administration, and a ClinicalTrials.gov search on 27 October 2026 found no registered studies, though that cannot exclude other registries or unregistered work.
cards.quote: No peripheral GABA-A therapy for tactile over-reactivity in autism has been approved.
cards.section: What this does and does not mean for people

cards.front: Part of a tactile phenotype in these models begins outside the brain. Why does that not make autism a peripheral condition?
cards.back: The manipulations are mouse sufficiency tests, the behaviours are operational assays rather than experiences, and the rescue experiments left major features unchanged.
cards.why: Sufficiency under a restricted manipulation does not make the targeted population the only route, and human differences are task-specific and run in both directions.
cards.quote: The manipulations are mouse sufficiency tests, the behaviours are operational assays rather than experiences, and the rescue experiments left major features unchanged.
cards.section: What this does and does not mean for people

cards.front: You plan to delete Gabrb3 in sensory neurons with a tamoxifen-inducible driver in defined windows. Which littermate controls must the design include, and why?
cards.back: Tamoxifen-treated Cre-negative and untreated Cre-positive littermates, because inducible drivers can recombine without ligand to an extent that varies with driver, tissue and age.
cards.quote: Include tamoxifen-treated Cre-negative and untreated Cre-positive littermates, because inducible drivers can recombine without ligand
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: To test whether early tactile over-reactivity causes later anxiety-like behaviour in mice rather than merely predicting it, why must both readouts be taken from the same animals?
cards.back: Measuring air-puff reactivity at P4 and the later anxiety-like and social assays in the same animals makes each animal supply both ends of the association, so the link is within an animal rather than across genotypes.
cards.quote: Measure air-puff reactivity at P4 and the later anxiety-like and social assays in the same animals.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Besides static detection thresholds, Puts and colleagues measured amplitude and frequency discrimination. What did those two measures show?
cards.back: Baseline amplitude discrimination was worse in the autistic cohort, while frequency discrimination showed no significant diagnosis effect.
cards.quote: Baseline amplitude discrimination was worse in the autistic cohort, while frequency discrimination showed no significant diagnosis effect.
cards.section: Human psychophysics beyond the mean

cards.front: Other human studies report lower thresholds at 200 hertz but not 30 hertz, and heightened forearm vibration sensitivity with normal light-touch thresholds. How should the Puts threshold result be held?
cards.back: As one result among inconsistent ones, because threshold findings vary with frequency, body site and age.
cards.quote: Threshold findings vary with frequency, body site and age, so the Puts result is one result among inconsistent ones.
cards.section: Human psychophysics beyond the mean

cards.front: A dorsal-horn miniature-current comparison reports seven cells per genotype, drawn from two mice per genotype. What is the largest n you may claim for animals, and why?
cards.back: Two per genotype. Cells from one mouse share genotype, litter, preparation and day, so seven cells are not seven independent animals.
cards.quote: Cells from one mouse share genotype, litter, preparation and day, so seven cells are not seven independent animals.
cards.section: Recording details behind the timing map
